brief.analysis: Defense stocks have outrun the market on a durable NATO spending surge — European budgets up about 20% in a year and every ally now meeting its target — so the underlying fair value is genuinely climbing. The engine's own trend-adjusted reading confirms this: measured against its rising trend the pair is barely stretched, disagreeing with the raw signal by more than a full step, which is direct evidence the average itself is drifting up. With the trend intact and no confirmation, the five-year average is an invalid, backward-looking target.
brief.report_line: Short defense-vs-S&P: avoid — the pair's own trend-adjusted reading shows it is barely stretched once you account for a rising, structurally-driven defense-spending trend, so the old average is drifting up under us.

brief.analysis: This is the clearest broken band: chipmakers have run far ahead of the broader Nasdaq on a genuine, multi-year AI build-out with hyperscalers committing on the order of a trillion dollars a year in spending. Chips have barely pulled back and still sit well above where they were, and the old five-year average sits an implausible two-thirds below today's level. That five-year average is a relic of a pre-AI world and is not a real target; betting on a full return to it is fighting the biggest capital-spending cycle in the market.
brief.report_line: Short chips-vs-Nasdaq: avoid — the AI spending boom has permanently repriced semiconductors, so the five-year average target is a statistical mirage rather than a level the pair will revisit.

brief.analysis: The strongest case for a permanent shift is that record central-bank gold buying has become a lasting feature, not a blip, and gold beat stocks by an unusually wide margin in 2025. But this trade has already done its work: gold has pulled back toward its one-year average, which is the target the engine actually cares about and which its five most recent look-alikes all reached. The realistic profit target is that one-year average, not the flat five-year average, which the gold buying story has likely dragged permanently higher.
brief.report_line: Short gold-vs-S&P: gold has already snapped back to its one-year average and history favors more, but structural central-bank buying means we anchor to that average, not the richer five-year one, and size accordingly.

brief.analysis: Silver ran violently ahead of gold and has already snapped most of the way back to its one-year average, which the engine's confirmation signals fully support. The regime worry is real: silver is in a multi-year physical shortage driven by solar and electronics that has quietly lifted its fair value versus gold. Trade the reversion to the one-year average, but treat the much lower five-year average as a moving target that the supply deficit has likely pushed permanently higher.
brief.report_line: Short silver-vs-gold: the violent overshoot has largely corrected to the one-year average, but a structural silver shortage means we stop there and do not chase the stale, deeper five-year target.

brief.analysis: Metals and mining shares spiked far ahead of the market and have already reverted to their one-year average, the level both look-alike episodes reached. The regime risk is a broad commodity up-cycle — copper hitting records on structural shortages alongside gold — that plausibly lifts the group's fair value. Play the reversion to the one-year average, which is done, but do not count on the deeper five-year average, which the commodity cycle may have moved permanently higher.
brief.report_line: Short metals-and-mining-vs-S&P: the spike has already reverted to the one-year average, so we bank that and size down rather than betting on the stale five-year target amid a live commodity up-cycle.
